How old is Koh Samui as a destination? | Tourism on Samui is about 50 years old. Backpackers began arriving in the 1970s, soon after the first roads were built, simple bungalows followed at Chaweng in the late 1970s and 1980s, and mass tourism grew after the airport opened in 1989.
Why is Koh Samui called the coconut island? | Because coconuts were its economy for generations. From the 19th century Hainanese Chinese settlers planted coconut and cotton and shipped the crop to the mainland, and coconut palms still cover much of the lowland today.
When did tourism start on Koh Samui? | In the 1970s, when the first Western backpackers arrived by boat and stayed with local families. Modern tourism picked up pace in the late 1970s, and the Tourism Authority of Thailand launched a master plan for the area in 1985.
When was Samui airport built? | Samui Airport opened in 1989. Bangkok Airways built it, and an expansion to 11 gates and 6 million passengers a year is planned for completion in 2030.
Who owns Samui airport? | Bangkok Airways, which built the airport and has owned and run it since it opened in 1989. That is why it has an open-air terminal and why the airline operates most flights to the island.
Is Koh Samui a city? | Yes, administratively. The whole island became one city municipality, Thesaban Nakhon Ko Samui, in 2012, after being a subdistrict municipality from 1999 and a town municipality from 2008. It is also a district of Surat Thani province.
Where does the name Samui come from? | Nobody knows for sure. Theories link it to a local tree called ton samui, to a Hainanese word, to the Malay word for a safe haven, or to a Sanskrit or Tamil term for sea weather, but none has firm evidence.
Who were the first people on Koh Samui? | Bronze drums found in the southern hills suggest people lived here more than 2,000 years ago, and local tradition says fishermen from the Malay Peninsula settled in around the 6th century. Hainanese Chinese traders followed in the 19th century.
When were the roads built on Koh Samui? | The island had no roads until the early 1970s; villages were linked by footpaths and boats, and crossing it could take a day. Those first roads grew into today's 51 km ring road.
